Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn A Romanian F-16 aircraft shot down a drone on Sunday, July 26. It was the third time that this happened in three consecutive days, after similar incidents on Friday, July 24, and Saturday, July 25. The drone was shot down at 10:13 AM, July 26, above Romania’s territorial waters, in the Sulina–Chilia area, according to Romanian president Nicusor Dan. The president’s announcement came about half an hour after the drone was shot down. “I congratulate the Romanian pilots and the ground crews for the professionalism, courage, and efficiency with which they carry out their missions. Through their actions, they contribute to the defense of the national territory and the safety of Romanian citizens,” he stated on Facebook . Dan specified that the first drone shot down on Friday was a Shahed model used by the Russian military and said that Romania will initiate a diplomatic protest against Russia. “According to the investigation carried out by the General Prosecutor’s Office, the drone shot down on Friday morning is a Shahed type, used by the Russian Federation in its war of aggression against Ukraine. The investigations into the drones shot down yesterday and today are ongoing. Romania’s diplomatic protest against the Russian Federation will be based on these investigations. It is unacceptable and intolerable for the Russian Federation to continue violating Romania’s airspace, which is at the same time NATO and European Union airspace,” he added. The drone was neutralized “under safe conditions,” at a distance of approximately 12 kilometers northeast of Sulina, above Romania’s territorial waters, the Ministry of Defence also said in its press release. The institution noted that “four of the five drones shot down so far on the territory of EU countries in NATO have been neutralized by Romanian military pilots.” Back in May, a Romanian F-16 Fighting Falcon fighter jet deployed as part of NATO’s enhanced air policing mission in the Baltic region shot down a drone in Estonian airspace . Since the outbreak of the war in Ukraine, more than 100 attacks have been recorded on Ukrainian territory near the border with Romania. During the same period, 33 incursions of Russian drones into Romania’s airspace were recorded. Authorities have also identified drone fragments or entire drones on Romanian territory in approximately 50 cases. The most recent incursion sparked reactions from the Romanian government, which has upped spending on defense in recent years . Interim PM Ilie Bolojan condemned the drone incursion, emphasizing that the incidents of recent days are the consequence of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. Interim foreign minister Oana Ţoiu, in turn, announced that the Russian ambassador to Bucharest had been summoned to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs following the repeated violations of Romania’s airspace by the Russian Federation. radu@romania-insider.com (Photo source: Ministerul Apararii Nationale, Romania - www.mapn.ro ) Read next 24 July 2026 Defense Update: F-16 downs drone in Romania's airspace for first time Normal Defense Romanian Air Force shoots down three drones in three consecutive days 26 July 2026 Radu Dumitrescu Like this article? Photograph: Brais Lorenzo/EPA Books ‘It is not only a future certainty – the disaster is already here’: why we need climate fiction As wildfires rage across Europe and Britain swelters through its hottest summer on record, literary fiction has a vital role to play in capturing the severe consequences of climate crisis Tara Menon Sun 16 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 10.06 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google E arlier this summer, I travelled through Europe on a book tour. Everywhere I went, the heat broke records. In Italy, Germany and Spain, I sought refuge from the afternoon sun in air-conditioned hotels. In normally temperate Zurich, it averaged 37 degrees. I jumped into the Limmat for relief. On my final day in Warsaw, Poland had never been hotter – one of 14 countries to hit a historic high. In June, when I left to return to the US, Europe was scorching. At the end of July, as I write this, it is burning. Since the heatwaves began, there have been more than 10,000 excess deaths. Yet for many, myself included, the high temperatures brought nothing more than inconvenience – uncomfortable commutes, heat rash, less time outdoors. This seems to be a defining feature of today’s climate crisis; deadly for some, banal for others. Even when the world is on fire, it somehow doesn’t feel like an emergency for everyone. This disparity cast my mind back to Hurricane Sandy in 2012 . I was living in New York, one of millions ordered to shelter in place. (I was lucky – hundreds of thousands were ordered to evacuate their homes.) I followed instructions. I stayed in my warm, dry apartment on the Upper West Side, watching trees swaying violently against the dark sky. The next morning, the rain had stopped; the sun was out, the air was still again and the power was still on. When I went outside to survey the damage, there was little to see except a few broken branches. The mood in my neighbourhood was jovial. The subways were closed, schools were shut, work was called off. Brunch was on. In other parts of the city, it was a different story. Whole fleets of taxi cabs submerged in water, their canary yellow roofs peeking out; a huge midtown crane snapped cleanly in half; the collapsed wall of an apartment building. I watched and rewatched a video of a power plant exploding. Half a million people, including most of the residents of lower Manhattan, were now without electricity. The American news outlets focused almost exclusively on New York. The international news sites told a more complete story: Sandy killed 233 people in eight countries and caused $70bn in damage. Several days after the storm, I volunteered in Chinatown, distributing basic goods – batteries, canned food and bottled water – to elderly people who lived on the highest floors of public housing buildings and hadn’t yet ventured outside since the storm. (the lifts weren’t working and they weren’t able to take the stairs). The apartments smelled of rotting food and unflushed toilets. The national guard rolled through the streets in tanks; rats brazenly stalked the pavements and Red Cross workers posed for photographs with locals. Research labs at NYU lost their lab animals during the storm; the news reported them dead, but rumours spread that the rodent population of the city had grown by 10,000 transgenic mice and rats. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Bookmarks Discover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to you after newsletter promotion In the weeks after Sandy, I was struck by the disparity between those who could escape the city to second homes and those who had nowhere else to go New rules governed downtown life. Bars served free drinks by candlelight, neighbourhood people with handmade signs offered water to passersby, small shops offered free charging stations. The roads around Ground Zero stayed flooded for weeks; the water was green and brackish. Amid the darkness, one building stayed lit, its squares of gold stretched into the sky. Goldman Sachs would not be stopped. In the days and weeks after Sandy, I was struck by many disparities: between downtown darkness and uptown light; between those who were able to escape the city to second homes and those who had nowhere else to go; between the countries with a quick, organised disaster response and those that relied entirely on community help. I also found myself thinking about the natural disasters I had heard about as a child and teenager growing up in Singapore: the 1999 Odisha cyclone, the 2003 heatwave across India, the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, the 2006 Southern Leyte mudslide in the Philippines, the 2007 cyclone in Bangladesh. These were disasters with much higher death tolls that I realised many people had never heard about. When Sandy made landfall in 2012, I had just begun my PhD in English literature. For work, I read canonical 19th-century realist novels; for pleasure, I read contemporary literary fiction. I searched for novels about the environment but often found myself disappointed. In many, the severe consequences of the climate crisis were packaged as a future possibility – something to come, one day. But the climate crisis is not only a future certainty, it is past and present truth. The disaster is already here. Can literary fiction capture both the freak event and the mundane truth of the climate crisis? Several years after Sandy, I read Amitav Ghosh’s The Great Derangement, in which he argues that literary fiction has failed us. Ghosh perfectly articulated my disappointment about the climate fiction, or cli-fi, I had read. But he went further. Ghosh listed the reasons the modern novel was unsuited to the challenge of representing the climate crisis. One, contemporary western novels had become “ever more radically centred on the individual psyche”. Two, unlike other genres, novels can’t range freely over space and time. Three, our literary imagination had become “radically centred on the human”. And four, the climate crisis is defined by improbable events and “probability and the modern novels are twins”. When I first read The Great Derangement, I agreed with Ghosh that “the climate crisis is also a crisis of culture, and thus of the imagination”. But I also wondered whether it would be possible to write what he said didn’t exist but should: serious literary fiction that captures both the freak event and the mundane truth of the climate crisis. Ghosh laid down a gauntlet; I thought I’d try to pick it up. Over the next eight years, I wrote a novel that moves towards two cataclysmic events – Hurricane Sandy and the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami – but also documents the slow violence that unfolds in both New York and Thailand. My debut novel, Under Water, seeks to represent climate change in the very form Ghosh suggests is ill-suited to the task: a realist novel centred on a single individual. It is true, as Ghosh notes, that, unlike epics, novels do not usually bring multiple universes into conjunction. But a realist novel centred on a bourgeois subject in today’s globalised world can in fact move across space and time. A single individual might, as my protagonist Marissa does, grow up on a barely inhabited island in south-east Asia and then, a decade later, live as an adult in a large metropolis on the east coast of the United States. My book also responds to Ghosh’s striking claim that the modern novel was “never forced to confront the centrality of the improbable”. In Under Water, I try to imbue Hurricane Sandy, a highly improbable event, with expectation. Because of her childhood and her past, Marissa experiences the approach of Sandy differently from other inhabitants of the city. Under Water is a riposte to Ghosh’s claim that the contemporary realist novel is destined to fail us. A single novel cannot show everything, everywhere, all at once. But it can, more effectively than any other cultural form, wield what I think is still one of our best weapons against this or any other crisis: the determination to pay close, careful attention to the people and places we are losing, every day. https://humanevents.com/2026/09/26/antif.text: http://humanevents.com/2026/09/26/antifa-militants-assault-professor-during-lecture-in-belgium-over-his-research-into-military-ai NEWS & ANALYSIS Antifa militants assault professor during lecture in Belgium over his research into military AI "We, VC(P)E-ULiège, staged this pie-throwing incident to ridicule Damien Ernst." by: Thomas Stevenson 09/26/2026 09/27/2026 "We, VC(P)E-ULiège, staged this pie-throwing incident to ridicule Damien Ernst." A professor in Belgium was assaulted by a group of Antifa radicals on Thursday during a lecture at around 2 pm at the University of Liège. He was teaching at the university's Montefiore Institute at the time of the attack. Damien Ernst, a prominent engineer and energy expert, was seen on footage getting assaulted by several masked Antifa members as he was speaking to the class present. The professor was shown on the viral video getting cream pies thrown on his upper body and face over his research on using AI in the military. Ernst said after the incident that he feared for his life, according to the Hungarian Conservative . Soon after the attack, a group that calls itself the " Vrai Comité (Populaire) d’Éthique de l’ULiège" or "Real Popular Ethics Committee of the University of Liège," claimed responsibility for the assault and accused the professor of collaborating with the military industry and creating AI for military purposes. The group said in a statement translated from French, "We, VC(P)E-ULiège, staged this pie-throwing incident to ridicule Damien Ernst—Wallonia’s most moronic engineer—and to highlight the array of harmful practices he embodies; we also sought to shame the University of Liège for organizing what can only be described as a criminal conspiracy—namely (and at the very least) the collusion between scientific research and the arms industry." The professor thought that it was a student prank at first before it became serious. The incident follows a far-left campaign against the defense industry; the University of Liège has been in a major research partnership with Thales, the French defense and aerospace group. Credit: AP/Kay Nietfeld By The Associated Press Updated October 11, 2026 11:18 am Share WARSAW, Poland — A man suspected of threatening and planning to attack Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk was arrested, the country's interior minister said Sunday. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński gave no details about the identity of the man nor the type of attack planned. Poland has been on high alert following a series of school stabbings this week, as well as fears of a possible Russian hybrid attack to weaken Western support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow’s full-scale invasion. “The man who threatened an attack was detained,” Tusk wrote on X. “Thanks to the police for fast and decisive action.” Poland's police had said earlier on Sunday they received information about a possible plot to attack Tusk and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. Sign up for the Breaking News newsletter Get the latest breaking news as it happens. By clicking Sign up, you agree to our privacy policy . “We take this matter extremely seriously,” said Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesperson for the minister overseeing Poland's intelligence services. He said authorities considered there was a “high probability” the threats would be carried out. Dobrzyński was speaking after an emergency meeting of security services, police and representatives of the Interior Ministry on Sunday. He said information about the threat first reached the state protection service, which then passed it to the police. He gave no other information about the reported plot, but said the intelligence services were receiving an increasing number of various threats with every month. Government spokesperson Adam Szłapka told Polish media Tusk learned about the threat first thing on Sunday morning. He said that, even if officials do occasionally get threats, this one was “exceptionally concerning.” Three attacks at schools in Mazovia province in central Poland took place within four days this week, leaving one dead and many wounded, including children. In September, Tusk warned about likely intensified hybrid attacks by Russia on NATO’s eastern flank. He said Russia was planning strikes with drones or rockets on European countries supporting Ukraine, among them Poland, with the goal of weakening Western support for Kyiv's fight against the Russian invasion. Moscow has denied any such plans.
